newsitem.title: UK: European gas giants disagree on EU directive.
newsitem.headline: European gas giants disagree on EU directive.

text.p: The European Union's proposed gas directive faces severe difficulties before a compromise can be reached which will satisfy all member states, senior officials of three of Europe's largest gas companies told a British government enquiry.
The directive, expected to be approved by the end of this year, is intended to open European markets to competition by gradually allowing consumers to buy gas from competing suppliers.

But gas sectors are at differing stages of development in each member state. And there are key differences between countries which produce some or all of their own gas and those which import nearly all of it.

But giving evidence to a committee examining the draft directive in the U.K.'s upper House of Lords on Thursday, Georges Bouchard, vice president and Head of European Affairs at Gaz de France said a compromise was better than nothing.
"We think it is better to have a directive which not everybody likes than no directive," he said.

He said that since an electricity directive was approved last year, it would be difficult to keep out a gas directive. This would be desirable as long as it allowed countries to develop their markets separately, and contained protection for long term take or pay contracts.
Wilfried Czernie, senior general manager of Germany's Ruhrgas warned of possible large-scale intervention in the industry by the European Commission
"Our minister of economics started in September last year with the attitude that there is no necessity for the gas directive at all," he said.
Bouchard said the main problem was that there was not a real market in Europe at present.
"You need many sellers and many buyers," he said. "But we only have four sellers."
The biggest suppliers to the European market are currently Russia, Norway, Algeria and the Netherlands.
Britain will also become a net exporter next year when the Interconnector, a pipeline connecting it with Zeebrugge in Belgium, comes onstream.
Pedro Moraleda, Director of International Relations at Spanish utility gasNatural said that for Spain's concern was the issue of long term take or pay contracts.

Spain, which takes most of its dry natural gas from Algeria through the Maghreb-Europe pipeline, wants such contracts protected, but many may be considered incompatible with competition under the directive.
Bouchard echoed this point, saying that Gaz de France buys 90 percent of its gas under take or pay contracts. This could cause it problems if it is forced to give up part of its market share
"If we lose more than 10 percent of our market we will have problems with take or pay contracts," he said, although he acknowledged that "for the consumer, more competition is generally good."
The directive is expected to open markets in three tiers, with the first granting large industrial users the right to buy from any supplier first -- although it is not yet agreed who
